summary: Redwood ran a model catalog walkthrough focused on selecting open models for SilverCrest's clinical summarization pipeline. Discussed benchmark expectations (latency, p99), compatibility matrix across quantization and target GPUs, and trade-offs between hosted API vs Dedicated/Private deployments. transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-09-01
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Dr. Anita Patel (CTO - SilverCrest), Sam Rivera (Head of ML), Jared Kim (SRE)

0:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we got about 45 minutes. We'll run through the model catalog demo, show how you pick open models, the benchmark profiles, and the compatibility matrix in the console. Liam will jump into the live console and a few perf slides.
0:18 Anita: Sounds great, we've been evaluating a bunch of open models for our clinical note summarization, main constraints are p99 latency under 800ms for short notes and cost per 1k tokens. Also need SOC 2 logs and KMS.
0:30 Liam: Cool, we built the catalog to make that decision easier. You can filter by task, architecture, and performance profile. For example, for summarization you can filter to encoder-decoder or decoder-only depending on your prompt pattern. Also you can see precomputed bench profiles — p50, p95, p99 — on CPU and various GPU types.
0:55 Sam: Quick question — how accurate are those precomputed profiles? Our prompts are pretty long, like 1.5k tokens in some cases.
1:05 Liam: Good point. The profiles are based on representative runs, but we always recommend running an internal microbench with your prompt set. The console has a 'run on sample' feature, you can upload a CSV of prompts and we run it against hosted and your dedicated nodes if you have them. Note that long sequences switch kernel selection and affect KV cache behavior which changes throughput.
1:40 Maya: Also to add, the model catalog shows quantization compatibility right next to the model. We flag 8-bit and 4-bit support and whether the runtime has verified perf for that quantization on our common GPU families. Sometimes the model name in the wild is a little off — transcription sometimes shows model ids as like 'opt-... something' — so keep an eye on the model tags.
2:05 Anita: And the compatibility matrix — does it say which models support KV cache or streaming? Both are important for us.
2:15 Liam: Yes, the matrix columns include streaming, KV cache, max sequence length, context window, quantization support, and recommended kernels. We also include estimated memory footprint and a recommended batch size for typical low-latency setups. For example, a 4-bit quantized Llama-2 style model on A100 will have different kernel selection than an unquantized on H100.
2:45 Jared: From infra — if we go private, what does the onboarding look like? We need VPC peering, SAML SSO, and KMS. Also network egress rules.
2:58 Maya: Private deployments include options for VPC peering or private link and a customer-controlled control plane. KMS integrations are supported; we can share our security whitepaper and SOC 2 certs. For Dedicated, we offer reserved pools with predictable throughput and an SLA.
3:18 Sam: Competitors first — did you benchmark against Anthropic or OpenAI? We ran some tests internally.
3:28 Liam: We include selected public baselines in the benchmark sheet. Due to differing tokenization and model variants it's not apples-to-apples, but we provide normalized tokens/sec and p99 numbers for common sequences. In the console you can compare side-by-side: latency, token cost, and a 'compatibility' score for features like streaming and KV cache. Note: some names we pulled from open repos are slightly different — sometimes 'Anthro' shows up in transcripts — sorry transcription quirks.
4:05 Maya: I'm going to share a quick demo screen.
4:10 [screen share]
4:20 Liam: Here is the model catalog UI, left panel filters, center is models list, right side is an expanded profile. See this model 'redwood-llama2-13b-open' — it's marked 4-bit compatible, streaming enabled, p50=85ms p95=210ms p99=420ms on our dedicated A100 pool. We also show cost per 1k tokens for hosted and dedicated.
4:50 Anita: Those p99 numbers look good. Are those measured with batching disabled? We need single-request latency.
5:00 Liam: Yes these are single-request baseline numbers with an average prompt of ~350 tokens. For long prompts we include a separate bench. You can toggle sequence length in the bench widget.
5:20 Sam: If we quantize down to 4-bit do you preserve output quality? Our clinical summarization is sensitive.
5:30 Liam: That's the trade-off. Our Optimize tool can run an automatic quality audit: you supply a holdout eval set and we run quality regression detection across quantization and model variants. We flag BLEU/ROUGE style deltas and semantic drift signals. Typically 4-bit can be acceptable for many workloads but we recommend validation on your clinical set.
6:05 Anita: How hard is it to pin a model version? We want deterministic rollouts.
6:12 Maya: You can pin exact model versions in the deployment config and roll out via canary or A/B. The Console supports rollouts with automatic fallback to a compatible variant if the pinned model is out of capacity.
6:30 Liam: On the compatibility matrix, note the 'fallback compatibility' column — it lists which compatible variants can be used when a primary variant is unavailable. For example, if an H100-optimized kernel isn't available we'll fallback to A100-compatible with an estimated latency delta.
6:55 Jared: For private/on-prem: what telemetry do you ship? We need audit logs for every inference request, not the token content but metadata.
7:05 Maya: We provide audit logs, request metadata, and optional per-token cost attribution. Content can be redacted and you can enforce KMS encryption in transit and at rest. We will share our security docs after the call.
7:25 Sam: Can we run a proof-of-concept on dedicated with an initial 2-week pilot?
7:30 Maya: Yep that's common. We typically do a 2-4 week pilot with a small reserved pool and a benchmark run. Pricing and trial contract can be shared.
7:45 Liam: Back to the bench UI — here's the compatibility matrix download button. It exports a CSV with columns: model_id, arch, quantization, streaming, kv_cache, max_seq, recommended_kernel, estimated_memory_mb, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, cost_per_1k_hosted, cost_per_1k_dedicated. You can import that into your perf team's tools.
8:15 Anita: Nice. One more governance question: data residency — our data must stay in US-East region. How do you handle that?
8:25 Maya: We have region pinning for hosted and Dedicated can be provisioned in a specified cloud region. Private on-prem obviously keeps data local. We'll note in the contract.
8:35 Sam: For the benchmarks you mentioned, can Liam run them with our tokenization? We use SentencePiece variant.
8:43 Liam: Yes, bring the tokenization script or we can run on your side. Our bench runner supports custom tokenizers; it just needs the tokenized sequences and prompt/response lengths.
9:00 [Liam pulls up a sample CSV upload]
9:05 Liam: Upload sample prompts, choose target models, and run. It will give per-model latencies and a quality column if you upload reference summaries.
9:20 Anita: Do you have any recommended open models for clinical summarization that are known to have low hallucination?
9:30 Liam: We don't claim clinical accuracy, but models trained with instruction tuning and larger context tend to be more coherent. In our catalog we tag models with 'recommended for summarization' based on community evals and our own internal tests. The 'llama2-like' 13b and 70b variants show better ROUGE on clinical-like tasks in our benchmark set, but they also increase memory and cost.
10:05 Sam: Could you show the side-by-side compare feature?
10:10 Liam: Sure, selecting two models... here's the comparison. You can see p50/p95/p99, cost delta, feature support (streaming yes/no), and an estimated throughput curve. There's also a visual of latency vs sequence length — you can pick your 95th percentile sequence length from your upload and it will highlight expected latency.
10:40 Anita: Regarding rollouts, how do you handle model versioning when we retrain a proprietary fine-tune? We may bring in a fine-tuned variant.
10:50 Maya: For private or dedicated you can upload your model artifact to a secure bucket and register it in the catalog. You can tag it private. The Console will treat it as a catalog model and include it in compatibility checks; it will show quantization compatibility after we run a quick verification pass. There is a short onboarding process where our infra team validates kernel compatibility.
11:20 Jared: If we host a private variant, will Redwood still handle autoscaling? We want to avoid doing orchestration ourselves.
11:28 Liam: Yes for Private with Redwood-managed control plane we handle autoscaling and kernel scheduling. For pure air-gapped on-prem there is an ops package; autoscaling can be done but requires additional ops integration. We can send the detailed ops docs.
11:50 Maya: Okay quick recap and proposed next steps: Maya will send the model catalog PDF and security pack; Liam will run the benchmark with SilverCrest prompts and share the sheet; Jared will share infra constraints. We will schedule the infra deep dive next week. Any final questions?
12:12 Anita: No, that's it. Thanks, folks.
12:20 Maya: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

End of transcript.
